chapter_title: Basic Principles of Anchored System Design

sections.title: General Design Concepts for Anchored Walls
sections.summary: An anchored wall creates an internally stable soil mass secure against the failure conditions of Figure 11 with limited movement. Anchors transfer the required force behind the active zone (Figure 12a), and bond lengths must extend past deep potential failure surfaces with inadequate factors of safety (Figure 12b).
sections.body: The concept of an anchored wall system is an internally stable soil mass resisting external failure modes at adequate serviceability. Design aims for a final wall secure against a range of potential failure conditions (Figure 11, p. 27: (a) tensile failure of tendon; (b) pullout of grout/ground bond; (c) pullout of tendon/grout bond; (d) wall bending failure; (e) insufficient passive capacity; (f) forward rotation, cantilever before the first anchor; (g) insufficient axial capacity; (h) overturning; (i) sliding; (j) rotational failure of the ground mass), limiting soil and wall movement on a practical, economical construction basis, and considering mobilization of resistance by both anchors and wall elements. The total anchor force needed for equilibrium follows from soil, water and external loads; anchors transmit the stabilizing forces back into the soil at a suitable distance behind the active zone loading the wall (Figure 12a, p. 28), which generally sets the minimum distance behind the wall of the anchor bond length. The bond length must also extend to intersect potentially critical failure surfaces passing behind the anchors and below the wall base (Figure 12b); the required depth follows from the deepest potential failure surfaces with insufficient factor of safety without anchor force. In summary: the wall should support the soil immediately adjacent to the excavation in equilibrium, typically governing the maximum anchor force and wall dimensions, strength and bending moments; and the anchors should extend deep enough to act on the range of shallow and deep-seated surfaces with inadequate factors of safety so they reach an acceptable factor of safety. (pp. 26 to 28)
key_points: Design against the failure conditions of Figure 11 with limited movement (p. 26).
Anchor forces transmitted behind the active zone (Figure 12a) (p. 26).
Bond lengths intersect deep potential failure surfaces with inadequate FS (Figure 12b) (p. 26).
Wall support of adjacent soil governs anchor force and wall section (p. 26).

sections.title: General
sections.summary: For economy the designer specifies only the parameters needed for long-term stability and leaves anchor details to the contractor; each installed anchor is tested above its design load. The designer must consider the possible failure mechanisms.
sections.body: Many types of anchored systems can usually meet a project's needs. For maximum economy the designer should specify only the parameters needed for long-term stability and leave final selection of anchor details to the contractor. Performance is evaluated by testing each installed anchor at loads exceeding the design load. To decide what to specify, the designer must consider the possible failure mechanisms. (p. 28)
key_points: Specify only what long-term stability needs; contractor selects anchor details (p. 28).
Every installed anchor tested above design load (p. 28).

sections.title: Failure Mechanisms of the Ground Anchor
sections.summary: Anchor failures come from excessive static load. Tendon load at most 60 percent of SMTS in design and 80 percent temporarily; ground mass failure not a factor below 4.5 m; ground-grout bond mobilizes progressively, little gain beyond 9 to 12 m (Table 3); creep-prone soils (organic, LI > 0.2 by Eq. 1, LL > 50, PI > 20); grout-tendon bond by adhesion, friction, interlock (ASTM A981).
sections.body: Anchor failures are usually caused by excessive static loading from (1) tension during load testing or at lock-off, (2) excavation sequence, (3) surcharge by construction materials or equipment, (4) adjacent construction, or (5) a combination; mechanisms involve the steel tendon, the ground mass, the ground-grout zone and the grout-tendon zone. Steel tendon: failure is inevitable if load exceeds structural capacity, so the tendon load should not exceed 60 percent of the specified minimum tensile strength (SMTS) for final design and 80 percent of SMTS for temporary conditions (e.g., testing). Ground mass (p. 29): for shallow soil anchors, uplift of a soil mass in front of the bond zone then pullout, a shear surface resembling passive failure; practically not a factor for anchors embedded more than 4.5 m. Shallow rock anchors in sound bedrock fail along a cone at about 45 degrees from the anchorage, varying in fractured or bedded rock; rock mass failure seldom occurs below 4.5 m, the rock-grout or grout-tendon bond being much weaker than the rock. Ground-grout bond: skin friction depends on normal stress on the grout and adhesion and friction at the interface (underreamed anchors add base resistance); it mobilizes progressively from the loaded end along the bond length until the ultimate bond is exceeded at the far end and the anchor pulls out; improperly grouted anchors with grout between bearing plate and bond zone show no load transfer to the bond length. Table 3 (p. 30), small diameter anchors in uniform soil, cohesionless/cohesive: soil properties, friction angle and grain size distribution / adhesion and plasticity index; drilling, driven casing increases normal stress and friction / drilling without casing or with fluids decreases capacity; bond length, steady increase in capacity to 6 m with moderating increases to 12 m / steady increase for undrained strength less than 96 kPa; hole diameter, slight increase to 100 mm / increases to 300 mm; grout pressure, capacity increases with pressure / increases only with stage grouting, avoid high initial pressures; note: clean the hole and grout as quickly as possible after drilling. Increasing typical soil bond lengths beyond 9 to 12 m does not significantly increase resistance, possibly because upper interface resistance drops to residual; longer bonds need special procedures. Creep (p. 30): susceptible deposits are (1) organic soils, (2) clays with average liquidity index (LI) over 0.2, (3) clays with average liquid limit (LL) over 50, (4) clays with average plasticity index (PI) over 20; use conservative design loads and bond stresses for permanent anchors in them unless predesign or preproduction tests (section 5.3.6) justify otherwise. LI by Eq. 1: low LI means moisture near PL (potentially overconsolidated or stiff), LI near 1.0 near LL (potentially normally consolidated or soft). Grout-tendon bond (p. 31): adhesion, friction and mechanical interlock, the last dominant for threadbars; on smooth tendons bond mobilizes progressively, and after slip only friction (about half the maximum) remains. Bond is not linearly proportional to grout strength (e.g., 17.2 MPa bond for 27.6 MPa grout rises only 12 percent to 19.3 MPa when grout strength rises 25 percent to 34.5 MPa); added embedment adds bond at reduced unit values; flaky rust lowers bond but wiping the loosest rust gives a bond equal to or greater than unrusted bar; pitted bars cannot be accepted; loose powdery rust has no significant effect. Owners should request mill test reports for each lot, including strand bond capacity tests per ASTM A981 (1997, prompted by manufacturing residues reducing strand-grout bond). (pp. 28 to 31)
key_points: Tendon load at most 60 percent SMTS (design), 80 percent SMTS (temporary, testing) (p. 28).
Ground mass failure not a factor for anchors deeper than 4.5 m (p. 29).
Ground-grout bond mobilizes progressively; little gain beyond 9 to 12 m (p. 29).
Table 3: factors influencing bond stress transfer in cohesionless and cohesive soils (p. 30).
Creep-prone: organic soils, LI > 0.2, LL > 50, PI > 20 (p. 30).
LI = (wn - PL)/PI (Eq. 1) (p. 30).
Request mill test reports with ASTM A981 strand bond tests (p. 31).
equations: Eq. 1: LI = (wn - PL) / PI; liquidity index, where the moisture content of a clay falls between its plastic and liquid limits, wn = moisture content, PL = plastic limit, PI = plasticity index (p. 30)

sections.title: Failure of Soldier Beams
sections.summary: Soldier beam lateral resistance is most critical when testing the first anchor and at final excavation; apply a safety factor of 1.5 to passive resistance. No vertical load transfer above the excavation base is assumed (wall friction 0); below it, use deep foundation methods with the averaged effective stress and checked load sharing for lean-mix fill.
sections.body: Soldier beams take lateral and vertical loads from the retained soil and anchor prestressing. Lateral resistance is most critical during stressing and testing of the first anchor level, often at shallow depth with low passive resistance behind the beam (p. 32), and at final excavation. Deflections are limited in design by a safety factor of 1.5 on passive resistance and in construction by tight upper lagging and not removing soil behind the beam; at final excavation passive resistance in front must restrain the toe for long-term loads and future undercuts. Vertical load transfer above grade to the soil behind the beam is hard to estimate and creates a negative wall friction angle on the active block, raising earth pressure; the document assumes no load transfer (interface wall friction angle = 0 degrees) above the excavation base because relative movements are small, removing soil from the face may reduce the "bond", and the transferred load is usually small; other procedures may be used with documentation of the movements needed. Below the base, vertical capacity follows common deep foundation procedures, with two issues: excavation stress relief reduces effective stress on the embedded part, commonly taken as the average of the effective stresses from the retained height behind and the soil depth in front; and for sections in predrilled holes, structural concrete fill shares axial and lateral load (lateral capacity on the hole diameter), but with nonstructural ("lean-mix") concrete the shear capacity between steel and fill may not allow load sharing and should be checked. (pp. 31 to 32)
key_points: Most critical: first anchor testing and final excavation (p. 31).
Safety factor of 1.5 on passive resistance limits deflection (p. 32).
No vertical load transfer above the excavation base assumed (wall friction 0) (p. 32).
Effective stress below base: average of retained-side and front-side values (p. 32).
Check steel to lean-mix shear before assuming load sharing (p. 32).

sections.title: Failure of Lagging
sections.summary: Timber lagging usually carries temporary excavation loads only (pressure-treated lagging has carried permanent loads) and is excluded from the final facing design; it is sized from experience-based charts accounting for soil arching (FHWA-RD-75-130, 1976).
sections.body: Timber lagging generally supports only temporary loads during excavation, though pressure-treated timber lagging has supported permanent loads. Temporary lagging is not included in the structural design of the final wall face. It is not designed by traditional methods but sized from charts based on project experience that account for soil arching between adjacent soldier beams (FHWA-RD-75-130, 1976) (p. 33). The heading is printed "4.2.4.". (pp. 32 to 33)
key_points: Timber lagging usually temporary; excluded from final facing design (p. 32).
Sized from experience charts accounting for soil arching (FHWA-RD-75-130) (p. 33).

sections.title: General
sections.summary: Retained soil strength governs earth pressures, axial and lateral capacity of the embedded wall and external stability; emphasis is on temporary walls in soft to medium clays and walls in heavily overconsolidated stiff to hard clays.
sections.body: The section guides selection of soil shear strength parameters for anchored system design, needed to evaluate earth pressures on the wall, axial and lateral capacity of its embedded portion, and external stability. It emphasizes temporary walls in normally to lightly overconsolidated soft to medium clays and temporary and permanent walls in heavily overconsolidated stiff to hard clays. (p. 33)
key_points: Strength governs earth pressure, embedded capacity and external stability (p. 33).
Emphasis on soft to medium clays (temporary) and stiff to hard overconsolidated clays (p. 33).
sections.applicability: Shear strength selection for anchored wall earth pressure and stability analysis

sections.title: Drained Shear Strength of Granular Soils
sections.summary: Granular soil strength is the drained friction angle phi', estimated from SPT or CPT results since undisturbed sampling is difficult.
sections.body: The drained shear strength of granular soil is conventionally the drained effective stress friction angle phi'. Because undisturbed sampling of granular deposits is difficult, the design friction angle may be estimated from in situ penetration tests such as the SPT and CPT. (p. 33)
key_points: Drained friction angle phi' for granular soils (p. 33).
Estimated from SPT or CPT (p. 33).
sections.applicability: Shear strength selection for anchored wall earth pressure and stability analysis

sections.title: Undrained Shear Strength of Normally Consolidated Clay
sections.summary: Soft to medium clays contract in shear, generating positive pore pressures, so the short term undrained condition governs temporary walls. Prefer consolidated undrained triaxial tests with pore pressures; Su depends on test mode: compression for wall pressures, extension (or correlations) for toe capacity.
sections.body: Undrained instability develops mainly under contractive shear, typical of normally to lightly overconsolidated soft to medium clays: the tendency to contract cannot be realized at the rate of shearing, positive pore pressures reduce effective stress and frictional resistance, and short term undrained resistance is less than drained, so the short term condition is critical for temporary walls in these clays. Su may be found by in situ (CPT, FVT) and laboratory methods (Kulhawy and Mayne, 1990), typically triaxial tests on nominally undisturbed samples at natural water content; consolidated undrained triaxial tests with pore pressure measurement are preferred, unconfined and unconsolidated undrained tests possibly erroneous from disturbance and no reconsolidation. Su is not a fundamental property and depends on test mode, boundary conditions, loading rate, initial stress and other variables (p. 34), so the designer should consider how field strength differs from measured: for a temporary wall in soft to medium clay, earth pressures may use triaxial compression strength, but toe lateral capacity is better evaluated with triaxial extension strength, which better models excavation unloading, passive zone strength possibly being less than active zone strength in some clays; correlations can convert compression strength to other loading paths (Kulhawy and Mayne, 1990). (pp. 33 to 34)
key_points: Contractive shear: short term undrained condition critical for temporary walls (p. 33).
Prefer CU triaxial tests with pore pressure measurement (p. 33).
Su depends on test mode (p. 34).
Compression strength for earth pressure; extension strength for toe capacity (p. 34).

sections.title: Undrained Shear Strength of Overconsolidated Clay
sections.summary: Excavation in overconsolidated clay produces negative pore pressures and temporarily higher undrained strength, but fissures allow rapid local drainage, so design in overconsolidated clays should use drained, effective stress parameters.
sections.body: Under excavation unloading, clay tends to expand as it mobilizes friction; this is resisted by negative pore pressures that raise effective stress and resistance, so short-term undrained strength and stability of an overconsolidated clay potentially exceed the drained values. Temporary and permanent walls are commonly built in stiff to hard overconsolidated clays, often fissured, allowing relatively rapid local drainage along discontinuities, so the period over which enhanced undrained strength applies cannot be defined with certainty. Design analyses in overconsolidated clays should therefore use drained, effective stress parameters. (p. 34)
key_points: Excavation unloading gives temporarily higher undrained strength (p. 34).
Fissures allow rapid drainage (p. 34).
Design in overconsolidated clays with drained effective stress parameters (p. 34).

sections.title: Drained Shear Strength of Overconsolidated Clay
sections.summary: Drained stiff clay strength falls from peak to fully softened and, at large displacement, residual (Figure 13). Use zero cohesion for long-term walls in stiff to hard fissured clays unless local experience supports it; the fully softened strength is the conservative design value; residual where a failure surface exists (Stark and Eid, 1994).
sections.body: Figure 13 (p. 35) shows drained shearing of an overconsolidated stiff clay: relatively uniform displacement to the peak stress tau_p, then concentration on a newly formed failure plane and reduction to tau_d, approximately the strength of the same clay normally consolidated (the fully softened strength, as from laboratory consolidation of a slurry); in relatively high plasticity clays further displacement along a major discontinuity reduces it to the residual strength tau_r. The designer must choose peak, fully softened or residual strength. The extra peak strength from cohesion (c' in Figure 13) reduces rapidly with strain beyond peak, and flexible anchored wall deformations may reduce it appreciably, so unless local experience supports a reliable value, zero cohesion should be used for long-term (drained) analyses of walls in stiff to hard fissured clays; the conservative drained strength is the fully softened strength, from triaxial compression tests with pore pressure measurement. Residual strengths should be used where there is evidence of an existing failure surface in the clay (e.g., stabilizing an active landslide); Stark and Eid (1994) correlate residual friction angle with clay size fraction and liquid limit. (pp. 34 to 35)
key_points: Peak, fully softened and residual strengths (Figure 13) (p. 34).
Zero cohesion for long-term analyses in stiff to hard fissured clays (p. 35).
Fully softened strength is the conservative drained design strength (p. 35).
Residual strength where a failure surface exists (Stark and Eid 1994) (p. 35).

sections.title: Earth Pressures
sections.summary: Heading for earth pressures: general (4.4.1), active and passive (4.4.2), at rest (4.4.3) and the influence of movement (4.4.4).
sections.body: Heading for earth pressures: general (4.4.1), active and passive earth pressure (4.4.2), earth pressure at rest (4.4.3) and influence of movement on earth pressure (4.4.4); it has no text of its own. (p. 36)
sections.applicability: Earth pressure theory and apparent earth pressure concepts for flexible anchored wall design

sections.title: General
sections.summary: Walls resist earth and water pressures from soil weight, earthquakes and surcharges; active, passive and at-rest conditions are considered. Linear theory simplifies processes depending on movement mode, flexibility, soil properties, prestress and interface friction, so flexible anchored walls use semi-empirical apparent pressure envelopes.
sections.body: A wall system resists the lateral earth and water pressures behind it, earth pressures arising mainly from the retained soil's weight, earthquake ground motion and surcharges. Three conditions are considered: (1) active, (2) passive and (3) at-rest earth pressure. Simple linear active and passive pressures from theory considerably simplify complex processes depending on (1) mode of wall movement (rotation, translation), (2) wall flexibility, (3) soil stiffness and strength, (4) horizontal prestress in the ground and (5) wall/soil interface friction. For anchored walls with flexible elements, semi-empirical "apparent earth pressure envelopes" are commonly used. (p. 36)
key_points: Active, passive and at-rest conditions considered (p. 36).
Linear theory simplifies movement-dependent processes (p. 36).
Flexible anchored walls use apparent earth pressure envelopes (p. 36).
sections.applicability: Earth pressure theory and apparent earth pressure concepts for flexible anchored wall design

sections.title: Active and Passive Earth Pressure
sections.summary: For a smooth wall with level backslope (Rankine, Figures 14, 15), KA and KP by Eqs. 2 and 3; with c', Eqs. 4 and 5; undrained (phi = 0), KAT = 1 - 2Su/sigma_v and KPT = 1 + 2Su/sigma_v (Eqs. 6, 7). General cases: log-spiral charts (Figures 16, 17); Coulomb passive pressures are unreliable. Wall friction for passive pressure 0.5 to 1.0 phi', 0.5 phi' for sheet piles.
sections.body: Active and passive pressures are limiting horizontal stresses; for a smooth (zero wall friction) wall with a horizontal backslope (Rankine conditions, Figure 14, p. 37), an element under vertical effective stress sigma'v (Figure 15) can fail at B, the maximum horizontal stress, or at A, the minimum. The print ties both to outward wall movement: the maximum "when significant outward movement of the wall increases the lateral earth pressure in the soil at the base of the wall" and the minimum to "the outward movement which reduces the lateral earth pressures behind the wall" (p. 36, as printed). Figure 15 gives Eqs. 2 and 3 (p. 38), consistent with Rankine for cohesionless (c = 0) soil; for effective stress parameters phi' and c', Eqs. 4 and 5; for the undrained case (phi = 0, c = Su), the total stress coefficients of Eqs. 6 and 7, sigma_v being total vertical stress. Wall friction on active pressure is relatively small and often ignored; KA comes from the equations or, generally, the lower part of Figure 16 (wall inclination, p. 39) or Figure 17 (backslope inclination, p. 40), based on log-spiral failure surfaces; KP from their upper part. The Coulomb method (NAVFAC, 1982) gives reasonable KA but is unreliable for passive pressure, its planar surface being in error against log-spiral surfaces (p. 41), always giving higher passive pressures. Design wall friction for passive pressure in front of an excavation ranges from 0.5 phi' to 1.0 phi', depending on wall material, soil, construction and axial load transfer; 0.5 phi' is recommended for continuous sheet-pile walls; passive pressures for anchored walls are in section 5.5. (pp. 36 to 41)
key_points: Rankine: KA = (1 - sin phi')/(1 + sin phi') = tan^2(45 - phi'/2) (Eq. 2) (p. 38).
KP = (1 + sin phi')/(1 - sin phi') = tan^2(45 + phi'/2) (Eq. 3) (p. 38).
With cohesion: Eqs. 4 and 5; undrained: KAT, KPT = 1 -/+ 2Su/sigma_v (Eqs. 6, 7) (p. 38).
Log-spiral charts (Figures 16, 17) for general cases (p. 38).
Coulomb unreliable for passive pressure (pp. 38 to 41).
Passive wall friction 0.5 to 1.0 phi'; 0.5 phi' for sheet-pile walls (p. 41).
equations: Eq. 2: sigma'h(min) / sigma'v = KA = (1 - sin phi') / (1 + sin phi') = tan^2(45 - phi'/2); Rankine active earth pressure coefficient for a smooth wall with horizontal backslope in cohesionless soil, sigma'h(min) = minimum horizontal effective stress, sigma'v = vertical effective stress (p. 38)
Eq. 3: sigma'h(max) / sigma'v = KP = (1 + sin phi') / (1 - sin phi') = tan^2(45 + phi'/2); Rankine passive earth pressure coefficient, sigma'h(max) = maximum horizontal effective stress (p. 38)
Eq. 4: KA = tan^2(45 - phi'/2) - (2c' / sigma'v) tan(45 - phi'/2); active earth pressure coefficient for a cohesive soil with effective stress parameters phi' and c' (p. 38)
Eq. 5: KP = tan^2(45 + phi'/2) + (2c' / sigma'v) tan(45 + phi'/2); passive earth pressure coefficient for a cohesive soil with phi' and c' (p. 38)
Eq. 6: KAT = 1 - 2Su / sigma_v; total stress active earth pressure coefficient for the undrained case (phi = 0, c = Su), sigma_v = total vertical stress (p. 38)
Eq. 7: KPT = 1 + 2Su / sigma_v; total stress passive earth pressure coefficient for the undrained case (p. 38)

sections.title: Earth Pressure at Rest
sections.summary: At rest Ko = sigma'h/sigma'v = 1 - sin phi' (Eq. 8): 0.55 to 0.65 for normally consolidated clay, 0.4 to 0.5 for sands, up to 1 for lightly and 2 or more for heavily overconsolidated clays. At-rest pressures (zero movement) are not practical for flexible anchored highway walls.
sections.body: Sand or clay normally consolidated under no lateral deformation (vertical compression only) and incremental vertical loading experiences earth pressure at rest, with Ko closely matching the empirical Eq. 8. Ko is typically 0.55 to 0.65 for normally consolidated clay and 0.4 to 0.5 for sands; for lightly overconsolidated clays (OCR <= 4) up to 1; for heavily overconsolidated clays (OCR > 4) up to or greater than 2. At-rest design pressures are not typically used for anchored walls with steel soldier beams or sheet piles: they assume no lateral deformation, possibly appropriate for heavily preloaded stiff walls, but zero movement is not practical for flexible anchored highway walls. (p. 41)
key_points: Ko = 1 - sin phi' (Eq. 8) (p. 41).
Ko 0.55 to 0.65 (NC clay), 0.4 to 0.5 (sand); up to 1 (OCR <= 4), 2 or more (OCR > 4) (p. 41).
At-rest pressures not practical for flexible anchored walls (p. 41).
equations: Eq. 8: Ko = sigma'h / sigma'v = 1 - sin phi'; coefficient of earth pressure at rest for normally consolidated sand or clay (empirical) (p. 41)

sections.title: Influence of Movement on Earth Pressure
sections.summary: Top-down construction makes pressures differ from fully active: in a model wall 1.9 m high (FHWA-RD-98-067; Figures 18 to 22), cantilever stage triangular, stressing creates pressure bulbs (lock-off 75 to 100 percent of design load), excavation causes bulging and redistribution; the trapezoidal apparent envelope fits the final pressures. Weak ground may develop full active pressures.
sections.body: The stress distribution behind a wall depends on its deformation; with top-down construction cycles of excavation, anchor installation, prestressing and lock-off, pressures are typically not approximated by fully active (linearly increasing) conditions used for gravity or nongravity cantilevered walls: lower pressures over parts of the wall are offset by higher ones elsewhere, and where walls penetrate competent soils pressures are highest near the anchors and small along the embedded portion. A two-level model wall 1.9 m high with 0.38 m final toe embedment (p. 42; Figure 18; FHWA-RD-98-067, 1998) illustrates: cantilever stage, excavation just below the first anchor, pressures and deformation consistent with active (triangular) conditions above the excavation, a "fixed-earth support" condition (Figure 19); stressing the upper anchor (p. 43) pushes the beam against the ground, pressures possibly approaching full passive near the load, and at lock-off (typically 75 to 100 percent of the design load) a pressure bulb above active remains (Figure 20); excavation to the lower anchor (p. 44) bulges the wall, reducing pressure between the upper anchor and subgrade and redistributing load to the stiffer anchor and subgrade (Figure 21); at end of construction (p. 45) the lower anchor stressing makes a similar bulb and excavation to final grade bulges the wall between lower anchor and subgrade (Figure 22). The trapezoidal "apparent earth pressure envelope" in Figure 22 closely approximates the final pressures (chapter 5); fully active triangular envelopes would overestimate pressures near the subgrade, giving overly conservative bending moments and embedment, and underestimate anchor loads and moments at upper supports. The results apply to flexible walls in competent ground with load redistribution; walls in weak ground may rotate outward near the subgrade and develop full active pressures (chapter 5). (pp. 41 to 45)
key_points: Top-down construction departs from fully active pressures (p. 41).
Model wall 1.9 m high, 0.38 m embedment (FHWA-RD-98-067; Figure 18) (p. 42).
Stressing creates pressure bulbs; lock-off typically 75 to 100 percent of design load (p. 43).
Trapezoidal apparent envelope approximates final pressures (Figure 22) (p. 45).
Weak ground may develop full active pressures (p. 45).
